```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Every sampler in multiGGM (`"gwishart"`, `"ssvs"`, `"mghs"`) returns the same
family of posterior edge probabilities, for each group and for each pair of
groups. You select edges from them with a median-probability rule or with
Bayesian false discovery rate (FDR) control. The probabilities come from running
sums kept over every post-burn-in iteration, so they are available with
`save_draws = FALSE`, which is what makes fits with hundreds of variables
practical.

## What is available

| | G-Wishart, SSVS | mGHS |
|---|---|---|
| **Per group** | | |
| Structural | PIP, $P(G_{ij} = 1)$ | $P(w_{ij} > 0.5)$ and $E[w_{ij}]$ |
| Cut model | | $P(Z_{ij} = 1)$ |
| Magnitude | $P(|x_{ij}| > c)$ | $P(|x_{ij}| > c)$ |
| **Per pair of groups** | | |
| Structural | $P(G_s \ne G_t)$ | $P(S_s \ne S_t)$, $S = 1(w > 0.5)$ |
| Cut model | | $P(Z_s \ne Z_t)$ |
| Magnitude | $P(|D| > c)$ | $P(|D| > c)$ |
| Union | $P(G_s \ne G_t \text{ or } |D| > c)$ | $P(Z_s \ne Z_t \text{ or } |D| > c)$ |

Here $x$ is a precision-matrix entry or partial correlation (`scale`), $D =
x_s - x_t$, and $w = \lambda^2 / (1 + \lambda^2)$ is mGHS's shrinkage weight.
`edge_probs()` returns all of them as one tidy table; `edge_prob_matrix()`
extracts one as a matrix.

## An example with two kinds of difference

Two groups share a block of edges (C). Group 2 has lost a block of edges (A:
a structural difference) and has a block whose edges are 1.5 times stronger
(B: same edges, different strength).

```{r sim}
library(multiGGM)
p <- 15
edges <- function(nodes) cbind(nodes[-length(nodes)], nodes[-1])
A <- edges(1:4); B <- edges(6:9); C <- edges(11:14)
O1 <- O2 <- diag(p)
O1[A] <- 0.3
O1[B] <- 0.3; O2[B] <- 0.45
O1[C] <- 0.3; O2[C] <- 0.3
O1 <- O1 + t(O1) - diag(p); O2 <- O2 + t(O2) - diag(p)
set.seed(1)
X <- lapply(list(O1, O2), function(O) matrix(rnorm(3000 * p), ncol = p) %*% chol(solve(O)))

fit <- multiggm_mcmc(data_list = X, method = "ssvs", burnin = 300, nsave = 600,
                     seed = 1, save_draws = FALSE, diff_deltas = c(0.05, 0.1))
```

```{r compare}
ep <- edge_probs(fit, scale = "precision")
pairs <- ep[ep$type == "pair", ]
block <- ifelse(paste(pairs$i, pairs$j) %in% paste(A[, 1], A[, 2]), "A: deleted",
         ifelse(paste(pairs$i, pairs$j) %in% paste(B[, 1], B[, 2]), "B: scaled",
         ifelse(paste(pairs$i, pairs$j) %in% paste(C[, 1], C[, 2]), "C: shared", "null")))
aggregate(cbind(p_struct, p_exceed_0.1, p_union_0.1) ~ block, data = pairs, FUN = mean)
```

* The **structural** rule sees the deletion (A) but not the change in
  strength (B): the edge is present in both groups either way.
* The **magnitude** rule $P(|D| > c)$ sees B, and here also A, because a
  deleted edge changes by its full size.
* The **union** rule sees both, and is the natural choice when any kind of
  difference matters.

```{r select}
select_diff_edges(fit, rule = "union", c = 0.1, scale = "precision", alpha = 0.05)
```

Within one group, `select_edges()` works the same way:

```{r within}
select_edges(fit, group = 2, rule = "structural", decision = "median")$n_selected
```

## Median rule or Bayesian FDR

`decision = "median"` selects edges with probability above 0.5, the
median-probability model. `decision = "bfdr"` (default) selects the largest set
whose posterior expected FDR, the mean of $1 - \text{probability}$ over the
selected edges, is at most `alpha`; tied probabilities are kept together. Both
report the posterior expected FDR of the set they select. Either is only as
good as the calibration of the probabilities.

## Do not select by "the interval excludes zero"

It is tempting to call an edge differential when the credible interval of
$D$ excludes zero, or equivalently when the sign probability
$\max\{P(D > 0), P(D < 0)\}$ (column `p_sign`) is high. Under a continuous
posterior, $P(D = 0) = 0$, so this is not a probability that the edge differs.
An edge with the same true value in both groups still has an estimated $D$ of
sampling-noise size, and with enough data its posterior is narrow enough to
exclude zero. In a simulation with mGHS (p = 100, n = 1000 per group),
Bayesian FDR on the sign probability gave an achieved FDR of about 0.50 at a
nominal 0.05. The same applies to SSVS, whose spike is continuous, and to
G-Wishart edges present in both groups. `p_sign` is reported for description
only.

## Choosing c

The magnitude and union rules test $|D| > c$, so $c$ is the **smallest
difference worth detecting**, and the FDR they control treats true differences
below $c$ as nulls. Choose it on the scale of the question:

* On the partial-correlation scale, $c$ is directly interpretable (e.g. 0.1).
* It must be clearly larger than sampling noise in $D$, roughly
  $\sqrt{2/n}$ for a partial correlation; otherwise identical edges are
  flagged. In the example, $\sqrt{2/3000} \approx 0.03 < 0.1$.
* Thresholds are fixed at fit time by `diff_deltas`, because the running sums
  count exceedances during sampling. Pass a fine grid (e.g.
  `seq(0.02, 0.3, by = 0.02)`) if you want to choose $c$ afterwards. With
  `save_draws = TRUE`, any other $c$ can be computed from the draws.

## mGHS

Following Busatto & Stingo (2025), the shrinkage weight
$w = \lambda^2/(1 + \lambda^2)$ uses the local scale only. The horseshoe
shrinks null edges mainly through the global scale $\tau$, so for a null edge
$w$ stays close to its prior, under which $P(w > 0.5) = 0.5$. The structural
and cut-model probabilities are therefore near 0.5 for null edges, and the
authors' median rule $E[w] > 0.5$ (`rule = "median_shrinkage"`) has a high
false-positive rate (about 0.37 in their Table 1). For differential edges with
mGHS, use the magnitude rule.

## References

*Annals of Statistics*, 32(3), 870-897.

Busatto, C. & Stingo, F.C. (2025). Inference of multiple high-dimensional
networks with the Graphical Horseshoe prior. *Journal of Computational and
Graphical Statistics*. doi:10.1080/10618600.2024.2435480

Newton, M.A., Noueiry, A., Sarkar, D. & Ahlquist, P. (2004). Detecting
differential gene expression with a semiparametric hierarchical mixture
method. *Biostatistics*, 5(2), 155-176.
